title: The Portrait of the Fens Anew
premise: Quentin Sterling, a night-shift taxi dispatcher in the fenland town of Marsh Hollow, has spent five years quietly logging the town's secrets—until a package arrives containing the diary of Elowen Pryce, who vanished in 2019. The diary's final entries are dated after her disappearance, written in her hand, and they name people Quentin knows: his mentor, his landlord, and the police inspector who closed her case. As Quentin follows the diary's clues through drainage ditches, derelict eel-smokeries, and the town's oldest families, he discovers Elowen staged her own disappearance to escape a smuggling ring that includes the man everyone mourns as her grieving father. In the flooded chapel beneath the old sluice gates, Quentin finds Elowen alive but trapped by the ring's last loyalist, and must choose between exposing the truth that will shatter the town—or protecting the belonging he has finally found there. He chooses truth, and the fens give up their dead and their living alike.
about_author: Mirabel Okonkwo is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing provincial records before turning to fiction, a career that taught her how much towns bury in plain sight. She writes mysteries set in wet, liminal landscapes where geography keeps secrets as stubbornly as people do.

chapters.title: The Night Book
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. On a rain-slicked shift, Quentin logs fares and gossip with equal precision until a parcel addressed to 'the man who listens at night' arrives containing Elowen Pryce's diary—the case file he helped alphabetize five years ago. The final entry is dated three weeks after she vanished. Emotional beat: the thrill of purpose cracking open five years of careful numbness.

chapters.title: Entries After the End
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Quentin cross-references the impossible dates against his own dispatch logs and realizes the post-disappearance entries reference real events only insiders could know—including one of his own late-night calls. He visits Inspector Halloway, who dismisses him with rehearsed ease. Emotional beat: unease deepening into obsession; the first sense that the closure everyone trusted was manufactured.

chapters.title: What the Ditch Gave Back
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Following a diary clue to a drained ditch near the eel-smokery, Quentin finds a rusted lockbox holding Elowen's spare keys and a photograph of four figures on the sluice gates—one face scratched out. His landlord, Aldous Pryce, Elowen's father, watches him from the embankment and offers help that feels like surveillance. Emotional beat: dread braided with loyalty; Quentin owes Aldous his lodging and perhaps his life.

chapters.title: The Alphabet of Small Betrayals
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Digging through five years of archived fare records, Quentin maps a pattern: the same addresses, the same moonless nights, pickups no passenger ever claimed. The route traces back to the smokery—and to Halloway's private number. Emotional beat: the quiet horror of realizing his own meticulous filing was the conspiracy's best cover.

chapters.title: A Kindness With Teeth
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Aldous invites Quentin to dinner, grieving father to lonely dispatcher, and gently suggests the diary is a cruel hoax. That night Quentin finds his flat searched and the photograph gone—but a new diary page left behind, in fresh ink: 'Stop looking, or look all the way.' Emotional beat: betrayal; the warmth Quentin craved revealed as a leash.

chapters.title: The Fourth Figure
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. A retired ferryman, drunk and frightened, identifies the scratched-out face: not a conspirator but a witness—Elowen's cousin Tamsin, who 'moved away' in 2019. Quentin tracks Tamsin to a coastal caravan park where she confirms the smuggling ring and admits she helped Elowen stage the vanishing. Emotional beat: hope with a cost; every ally widens the target on Quentin's back.

chapters.title: High Water Mark
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Tamsin reveals the diary's coded margins point to the drowned chapel beneath the old sluice gates, accessible only at spring tide's lowest ebb—which is tomorrow night. Halloway intercepts Quentin at the archive, confiscates the diary, and warns him off with a threat dressed as concern for his job. Emotional beat: cornered resolve; Quentin copies everything from memory, the archivist's revenge.

chapters.title: The Chapel Under the Sluice
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. At low tide Quentin wades into the flooded chapel and finds Elowen alive, hiding in the crypt, too afraid of Halloway and her father to surface. But Aldous followed him—and the tide is turning. Emotional beat: awe and terror fused; the missing person is real, breathing, and furious at being found.

chapters.title: Rising Tide
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Climax. Trapped in the crypt as water climbs, Quentin bargains with Aldous while Elowen slips through a maintenance passage to raise the alarm. Aldous confesses the ring began as protection for the town's poorest families and rotted into greed; when Quentin refuses silence, Aldous falters rather than drown them both. Halloway arrives to arrest the wrong person; Elowen walks out of the dark and names names. Emotional beat: catharsis through flood—truth surfacing like the tide itself.

chapters.title: The Portrait, Signed
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Weeks later, the trials ripple through Marsh Hollow; some neighbors shun Quentin, others finally speak to him as one of their own. Elowen, free, paints the sluice gates at dawn—a portrait of the fens anew—and gives Quentin the finished diary, blank pages now. He writes the first line himself. Emotional beat: belonging earned not by keeping secrets but by telling the truth; bittersweet, open-armed ending.
